item.content:encoded:
Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero has declared the day after Thanksgiving - Black Friday - a government of Guam holiday, giving government employees an additional day off this week

In an executive order issued Monday, Leon Guerrero designated Nov. 27 as a government holiday. All executive branch departments and agencies will be closed that day, with the exception of essential personnel and operations deemed necessary by agency heads to protect public health, safety and welfare.

The governor said the additional holiday recognizes the work of public servants while allowing families more time to spend together during the holiday season.

Lt. Gov. Joshua Tenorio also encouraged residents to support local businesses over the extended holiday weekend and practice inafa’maolek by looking out for one another on the roads and in their neighborhoods.

Residents are encouraged to plan ahead for any government services they may need before the Friday closure.

item.title: Bill seeks to include charter schools in Guam Youth Congress

Shelly Calvo, whose committee held the hearing, introduced the proposed legislation by saying the measure “seeks to align the law with current edu
item.content:encoded:
More than 50 years after the Guam Youth Congress was formed, representatives want to update legislation to more accurately reflect the island’s education environment by including charter schools.

On Monday, senators heard testimony on Bill 375-38 . Sen. Shelly Calvo, whose committee held the hearing, introduced the proposed legislation by saying the measure “seeks to align the law with current educational terminology.”

“Statutory references to junior and senior high schools no longer reflect Guam’s current educational designations,” Calvo said. “The existing statute does not expressly provide for charter school representation, despite charter schools being recognized as a distinct component of Guam’s public education system.”

Members of the Youth Congress testified in favor of the bill.

Under the bill, makeup of the Guam Youth Congress would still be capped at 51, with village representation being unchanged.

For school representation, the bill would replace outdated junior and senior high school classifications with reference to “private, public and charter high schools.”

Schools with up to 1,000 students would get one representative, schools with more than 1,000 students would get two representatives, and Guam Community College and the University of Guam would each get three representatives.

item.content:encoded:
The U.S. military is seeking federal authorization to continue training and testing activities in waters surrounding Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands through 2034, a proposal that would allow the incidental disturbance of marine mammals during those operations.

The National Marine Fisheries Service published a proposed rule Nov. 18 in the Federal Register requesting public comment on a seven-year authorization covering military readiness activities in the Mariana Islands Training and Testing Study Area from July 2027 through July 2034.

The request was submitted by the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps on behalf of the Navy, Coast Guard, Army and Air Force under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. The authorization would cover military training and testing activities involving sonar, underwater detonations and vessel operations that could result in the incidental take of marine mammals.

The study area includes waters south of Guam to north of Pagan, extending east into the Pacific Ocean and west into the Philippine Sea, as well as a transit corridor linking the Mariana Islands and Hawaii training ranges.

Federal officials said the proposed rule includes mitigation measures designed to reduce impacts on marine mammals, including sonar shutdown zones, vessel-strike avoidance protocols, monitoring requirements and seasonal protections in biologically important areas.

The proposed authorization would replace the current seven-year permit, which expires July 30, 2027. Similar regulations have governed military training and testing activities in the Mariana Islands region since 2010.

Public comments will be accepted through Dec. 18 before NMFS decides whether to finalize the authorization.

item.title: Ukrainian drones hit a Russian warship at a naval base in Libya, Zelenskyy says
item.description: Updated November 23, 2026 at 8:32 PM ChST KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 23, 2026 at 8:32 PM ChST

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine carried out an attack on a Russian warship moored at a port in Libya, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, claiming that sea drones sank the navy vessel in a surprise assault the previous day.

Ukrainian forces deployed seven domestically made sea drones in the operation, which struck the Russian navy corvette in the Mediterranean, according to Zelenskyy. The ship was one of Russia's newest vessels, commissioned a year after Moscow launched the 2022 invasion of its neighbor, the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.

Russian officials made no immediate comment.

The operation, conducted some 2,400 kilometers (1,500 miles) from the front line in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv's forces.

Ukraine has at times blindsided Russia during the war with ingenious attacks that embarrass Moscow, such as Operation Spiderweb in June last year, when drones launched from trucks hit over 40 aircraft parked near air bases across Russia. Along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (almost 800-mile) front line snaking through eastern and southern Ukraine, Kyiv's cutting-edge drones and ground robots are helping hold back Russia's bigger army.

At the same time, Russia's strategic bombing of Ukraine has devastated the power grid ahead of winter and damaged civilian buildings.

A Russian strike on a five-story apartment block in a village near Kyiv killed 11 people, regional police said Monday. A 7-year-old child and a 79-year-old woman were pulled from the rubble after the Sunday morning attack, rescue services said.

Zelenskyy described Sunday's attack as "exemplary" and said "the targets we set were achieved."

"We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons," he said.

Ukraine has hit Russian oil refineries as far away as western Siberia and Russian warships in the Mediterranean, Zelenskyy noted in a live video address Monday to a meeting of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.

"We keep finding ways to get back on our feet after every Russian attack," Zelenskyy said.

Ukrainian forces also struck the Russian dry cargo ship MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said Moscow used to transport weapons, and destroyed a Ka-27 military helicopter in the attack, the Ukrainian leader said.

Ukrainian forces are operating in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, using the North African country's territory to strike a Russian tanker in the Mediterranean in March, according to Libyan officials.

The Ukrainian forces, most of them drone experts, were at the time operating mainly at an air base in the coastal city of Misrata, but also in other military facilities in the capital Tripoli and the coastal town of Zawiya, the officials told The Associated Press earlier this year.

Sunday's attack severely damaged the Russian corvette at the Benghazi Naval Base in eastern Libya, according to two Libyan officials.

Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the base early Sunday. Civil defense units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.

The vessel had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, a statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.

The government in eastern Libya sent a letter to U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres and the U.N. Security Council, calling for an international investigation into the potential use of western Libya to prepare and launch Sunday's attack.

Libyan officials who were briefed on the attack told The Associated Press that at least four drones were intercepted while two hit the corvette, which is designed to patrol coastal waters and escort other ships.

At least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded in the attack, one of the officials said.

The officials, affiliated with the self-styled Libyan National Army, which controls eastern and southern Libya, spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to talk with reporters.

Ambrey, a U.K.-based maritime security and risk intelligence firm, said that some of the explosions at the Benghazi Naval Base were likely caused by the detonation of ammunition on board the Russian warship.

Hours after the warship attack, another sea drone strike hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel sailing off Benghazi, the Libyan coast guard said.

Ukraine's Security Service, or SBU, described the operation as "unique." It said the cargo ship MV Angara was sanctioned and used to transport Russian military equipment, and the multipurpose corvette Merkury regularly escorted Russian naval convoys, including guarding the MV Angara.

The drones were delivered to a designated location and launched from a so-called "mothership" near the target, the SBU said.

A Ka-27 helicopter was on board the corvette and also went under, the SBU added.

Russian defenses tried from air, sea and land to hit the attacking drones, it said.

"Ukraine's defense forces have once again shown that the Russian navy and its logistics have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea," which borders both Russia and Ukraine, the SBU said.

item.title: Seniors embrace Tesla automated driving technology despite questions about safety
item.description: EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals. Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.
item.content:encoded:
EVERGREEN, Colo. — Joan Spalding has driven the steep, winding road that leads to her house outside Denver for more than 50 years. But these days, the 89-year-old barely touches the steering wheel or the pedals.

Instead she tells the car where she wants to go, and presses a button on the large touch-screen in the dashboard of her Tesla Model Y.

For all practical purposes, the car appears to be driving itself, navigating confidently on twisting roads through postcard valleys full of juniper and ponderosa pine.

"Now this is probably one of the narrowest roads," Spalding says, as the car pulls onto a dirt track that can barely fit two cars side by side, with a steep drop off to one side.

The Tesla handles the tight turns gracefully, even stopping to let an SUV squeeze by in the other lane.

Spalding was skeptical at first of what Tesla officially calls Full-Self Driving (Supervised), often abbreviated as FSD. It's a subscription service that drivers pay for, usually $99 dollars per month.

That was, until she saw what it could do.

"When I was driving," Spalding said, "I saw that the kind of things that it did were safer than what I would do."

There are more older drivers on the road than ever, and families often struggle with the question of when it's time to stop driving. Now, seniors are using emerging technology to stay behind the wheel longer, specifically automated systems made by Tesla. But safety experts worry the company may be over-selling what its cars can do.

"It's not a technology that I would drive with. It's not a technology that I would suggest that my loved ones use. I think it has a few safety gaps that just make me uncomfortable," said Bryan Reimer, a research scientist at MIT, who studies how drivers interact with technology.

It's hard to know exactly how many seniors are using Tesla's automated driving system, but the numbers may be growing. Overall, Tesla says FSD has more than 1.7 million active subscriptions , an increase of 67% from a year ago. If the car-maker knows how many of those subscribers are seniors, it isn't saying.

Riding along with Joan Spalding, it's easy to understand the appeal for older drivers. The car gives her mobility and freedom that she wouldn't have otherwise.

Before she got her Tesla, Spalding had gotten into a number of minor fender benders. Then, two years ago, she was in a serious crash while she was trying to make a left turn.

"I made a wrong decision. I wasn't focusing on what I should be doing … I was lucky," she said. "But I realized then that my abilities were not where I wanted them to be."

Her son Mike Spalding had known for a while that his mother's driving was getting worse. He was already driving a Tesla, and it was his idea to get one for her.

"It would be safer for mom if she was in a wreck because it's got all kinds of safety features. And then safer for people around her if we didn't have any more crashes. I've been driving one for years, and so I'd experimented with the Full Self-Driving and saw what it could do," Spalding said. "It's better than me."

Tesla agrees. The company claims that FSD is up to nine times safer than human driving. Tesla doesn't release much data about FSD, so it's impossible to independently verify whether its safety claims are true, Reimer said. He concedes Tesla's technology is impressive and is getting better all the time, but says it's not a replacement for a human driver — at least, not yet.

"Tesla has continually over-promised and under-delivered," Reimer said. "Full self-driving is not full self-driving, but yet the name feels so real."

If you read the fine print, FSD is not fully autonomous. The company always uses its full title — FSD (Supervised) — in official communications, to underscore the point. The driver is supposed to be paying attention at all times, in case the car encounters a situation FSD can't handle.

The problem, according to safety experts, is that human drivers tend to get complacent.

"It's good enough, often enough, where people go, 'The next time I'm in this similar situation, I know how it's going to behave,'" said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, the nonprofit funded by the insurance industry.

But Mueller worries older drivers won't be ready or able to take control of the car in an emergency.

"This can be a huge problem," she said. "Ultimately it is very unsafe if you have drivers who are not fully competent due to age-related impairments or decline."

Tesla did not reply to requests for comment.

The company has not said exactly how many senior drivers are using FSD to stay on the road longer, or even if that's something Tesla is tracking. But the company's CEO, Elon Musk, has encouraged the practice.

In a recent post on his social media platform X, Musk said that "Tesla self-driving gives mobility to seniors." Several times, he's amplified a video from a YouTube channel called TFLEV, featuring a 98-year-old man, who just bought his first Tesla.

"It has not made a mistake. And I've been driving it probably two or three months and it's not made an error in its driving, " the driver, Larry Dimmock, said in the video. "In fact, the other day it stopped. A chipmunk was crossing the road and there was no other traffic and it did not run over the chipmunk."

Musk reposted the video last month, saying, "At Tesla, we even care about the chipmunks." The clip has been viewed more than 3.5 million times.

"My moment of fame, I guess," Dimmock joked in an interview with NPR.

Dimmock says he's owned dozens of cars in his life, starting with a Ford Model A. He says he's still a pretty good driver at 98 — but not as good as his Tesla.

item.title: Let's talk turkey: Here's how Thanksgiving meal costs have changed this year
item.description: If you're planning to cook this Thanksgiving, you might not be so thankful for higher food prices. Grocery costs have risen nearly 22% over the past five years, according to federal data . Wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Trump administration's tariffs and severe weather across the globe have pushed up the price of food.
item.content:encoded:
If you're planning to cook this Thanksgiving, you might not be so thankful for higher food prices.

Grocery costs have risen nearly 22% over the past five years, according to federal data . Wars in Ukraine and Iran, the Trump administration's tariffs and severe weather across the globe have pushed up the price of food.

Still, food-price experts say it's unclear whether you'll be spending more dough this Turkey Day — and, if so, by how much.

The American Farm Bureau Federation estimates that the cost of Thanksgiving will be up more than 6% compared with last year, with staples like cranberries and dinner rolls boosting the overall cost.

The Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute found that drinks like sparkling water and wine have become more expensive but that the average Thanksgiving food bill will come in a little cheaper than last year, due in part to sales and promotions.

"But you have to be very disciplined," said Wells Fargo chief agricultural economist Michael Swanson. "You get the turkey at a great price, but then you might throw a bunch of stuff in the cart you didn't look at that carefully and find out you spent more money than you intended to."

Financial worries have pushed some people to shake up their Thanksgiving celebrations. In a recent survey by the website LendingTree, 53% of respondents said inflation was affecting their holiday plans or how much they expected to spend on the meal.

"They're doing everything from changing their food choices to couponing more and even cutting back on guests," said Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at LendingTree.

The survey also observed a drop in the percentage of people who said they might host Thanksgiving this year: 51% expect to have company over, down from 59% last year.

Shoppers say they still want to celebrate Thanksgiving, despite the price of groceries.

"It's too high," said Philadelphia resident Andre Andrews, who is retired. "Things are high, so much higher." Nevertheless, Andrews said he plans to smoke a turkey and a roast for the holiday, even though they cost him more than previously. "I can tell you this: I know it was more than it was last year," he said.

Schulz of LendingTree said those cooking on Thanksgiving can save money by sticking to a budget, shopping around for the best price and paring down the menu.

"Nobody wants to cut back on something as meaningful as a gathering of family and friends on Thanksgiving because it costs too much," he said, "but that's what a lot of people are facing right now."
